newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair defends Labour policy on unions.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair defends Labour policy on unions.

text.p: British opposition leader Tony Blair, on course to win the May 1 election, defended his party's labour union policy on Monday saying a Labour victory would not mean a return to the strike-bound days of the 1970s.

He dismissed allegations by the ruling Conservatives that a Labour government would dismantle trade union laws ushered in under former prime minister Margaret Thatcher and vowed that "strikes without ballots, the closed shop and all the rest" were things of the past.

"The essential trade elements of the trade union legislation of the 1980s will remain," he wrote in The Times. "The changes that we do propose would leave British law the most restrictive on trade unions in the Western world."
Blair described the Conservatives' attempts to revive fears of union strangleholds on industry as ludicrous and said neither the trade unions nor the Labour Party wanted to turn back the clock.

As he launched his campaign after the long Easter holiday dominated by the resignation of Sir Michael Hirst, chairman of the Scottish Conservatives, over claims he had had a homosexual lover, and amid calls for two other members of parliament to step down, Blair said Labour would like to do their best to keep the election positive.

The Conservatives were also trying to change tracks and refocus their campaign. After party members' best efforts to convince former minister Neil Hamilton and MP Piers Merchant that it was time to go, there were signs on Monday of a party climbdown after both insisted on staying.

Hamilton, is at the centre of allegations that Harrods store owner Mohammed Al-Fayed paid several MPs generously to ask parliamentary questions, and photographs of married Merchant kissing a 17-year-old nightclub hostess in a park were splashed across the front pages of most of the country's newspapers.
Major had hinted in a letter commending Hirst for stepping down for the good of the party that Hamilton and Merchant should do the same.
But after it seemed unlikely that either would, Dame Jill Knight, the vice-chairwoman of powerful Conservative backbench 1922 Committee, softened the party's position.

"We have a far better story to tell in the long run. Mr Jones in the High Street is far more interested in the economy and education for his children than who is having an affair," she told BBC radio.
"We are not going to fly in the face of British justice and say a man is guilty because allegations have been made against him," she added.
The Labour Party claimed the apparent about-face by the Conservatives on the future of the two men was symptomatic of the way Major behaves.
"John Major's handling of the Neil Hamilton affair tells you all you need to know about his weak, dithering leadership," Deputy Labour Party leader John Prescott said in a statement.
"It is a story of drift, dither and total failure to achieve his objectives."
Major announced the election date on March 15, giving an unusually long 6-1/2 weeks notice of polling day, which he hoped his party would use to break down Labour's 20-point lead in opinion polls.

But almost since day one the Conservatives have been hit by a series of publicity disasters. As well as Hirst, one of their Scottish MPs has stepped down as a candidate amid rumours about his private life while former minister Tim Smith, implicated in the "cash for questions" affair, was disowned by his local party.
